Consistency Checks.Description: Study ID mismatch between summaries and reports
Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.6.5.1–2.6.5.7 (Toxicology written summaries; search for “Study ID”, “Study No.”, “Protocol”); Module 2.6.6.1–2.6.6.7 (Toxicology tabulated summaries); Module 4.2.3.1–4.2.3.7 (title page / cover page of each study report).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: Compare each study identifier (Study ID/number, sometimes protocol number) listed in Module 2.6.5.x and 2.6.6.x with the Study ID on the title page of the corresponding report in Module 4.2.3.x. Flag if any study in 2.6.5.x/2.6.6.x has no exact matching ID in 4.2.3.x or if 4.2.3.x contains major GLP studies not referenced in 2.6.5.x/2.6.6.x.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Traceability issue; reviewer cannot link summary conclusions to underlying GLP reports, leading to IRs or questions about completeness of the data set.

Consistency Checks.Description: Study title and test system description mismatch
Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.6.5.1–2.6.5.7 (study descriptions, “species”, “strain”, “duration”); Module 2.6.6.1–2.6.6.7 (tables listing species/strain/duration); Module 4.2.3.x (Study title, Summary, Methods).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: For each study, compare title descriptors (species, strain, route, duration) in Module 2.6.5.x and 2.6.6.x with those in the corresponding Module 4.2.3.x report. Flag if the duration (e.g., “4-week” vs “2-week”), route (“IV” vs “SC”), or species/strain is inconsistent.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Misrepresentation of study type or test system (e.g., calling a 2-week study “4-week”) can undermine confidence in the program and confuse dose/exposure arguments.

Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.4 (Toxicology overview – “GLP” phrases); Module 2.6.5.x (written, search for “GLP-compliant”, “non-GLP”); Module 2.6.6.x tables (columns for GLP status); Module 4.2.3.x Study reports (QA statement/GLP compliance sections).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: Compare GLP status text (e.g., “GLP”, “non-GLP”, “GLP-like”) in Module 2.6.5.x and GLP columns in 2.6.6.x against the QA/GLP compliance statement in each relevant Module 4.2.3.x report. Flag if a study labeled GLP in 2.6.x is clearly non-GLP in 4.2.3.x or vice versa.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Incorrect GLP designation can misrepresent regulatory robustness of the data set and impact the acceptability of pivotal safety studies.

Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.4, 2.4.5 (overviews – search “rat”, “dog”, “monkey”, etc.); Module 2.6.5.1–2.6.5.7 and 2.6.6.1–2.6.6.7 (species/strain/sex columns); Module 4.2.3.x (Methods – “Animals”, “Species”, “Strain”, “Sex”).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: For each study, compare species, strain, and sex distribution described in Module 2.6.5.x/2.6.6.x with the animal description in the relevant Module 4.2.3.x Methods sections. Flag if the species or strain is different (e.g., “Sprague–Dawley” vs “Wistar”) or if sex (male/female/both) is misreported.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Misstating species/strain/sex may distort interpretation of sensitivity, relevance, and exposure margins.

Consistency Checks.Description: Route and regimen mismatch (design vs summary)
Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.3, 2.4.4 (statements on dosing paradigms); Module 2.6.5.1–2.6.5.2 (single- and repeat-dose toxicity summaries); Module 2.6.6.1–2.6.6.2 (dose tables); Module 4.2.3.1–4.2.3.2 (Study design/Methods – “Route of administration”, “Dose regimen”).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: For each single- and repeat-dose study, compare route (IV, SC, PO, etc.), dosing frequency (QD, BID, weekly), and duration (days/weeks) in Modules 2.6.5.1–2.6.5.2 and 2.6.6.1–2.6.6.2 vs the design sections of corresponding Module 4.2.3.1–4.2.3.2 reports. Flag any mismatch (e.g., summary says 4 weeks, report is 13 weeks).
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Incorrect route or regimen undermines dose selection arguments, local/systemic toxicity relevance, and human translation.

Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.6.5.1–2.6.5.2 (text; search “mg/kg”, “mg/m²”); Module 2.6.6.1–2.6.6.2 (dose tables); Module 4.2.3.1–4.2.3.2 (Tables listing dose levels in Methods/Results).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: For each study, extract dose levels (mg/kg, mg/m²) in Modules 2.6.5.1–2.6.5.2 and tabulated data in 2.6.6.1–2.6.6.2 and compare with the dose levels reported in Module 4.2.3.1–4.2.3.2. Flag any difference in numeric dose (e.g., 100 vs 30 mg/kg) or missing intermediate dose levels.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Wrong dose levels in summaries lead directly to incorrect NOAEL identification and exposure margin calculations.

Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.4, 2.4.5 (MTD, “high dose” rationale); Module 2.6.5.1–2.6.5.2 (discussion of “MTD”, “dose-limiting toxicity”, “DLT”); Module 4.2.3.1–4.2.3.2 (Discussion/Conclusions where MTD or high-dose justification is described).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: Compare MTD or “highest dose tested” described in Module 2.4.4/2.4.5 and 2.6.5.1–2.6.5.2 with the pattern of toxicity in Module 4.2.3.1–4.2.3.2. Flag if summaries claim MTD was reached but 4.2.3.x shows minimal toxicity at high dose, or if high-dose justification (e.g., limit dose 1000 mg/kg) is not supported by study design.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Mis-stated MTD or high-dose rationale can make the high dose appear adequate when it is not, triggering IRs or hold.

Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.3 (Nonclinical PK overview – “Cmax”, “AUC”, “t½”); Module 2.6.3 (PK written summary) and 2.6.4 (PK tabulated summary); Module 4.2.2.x (TK/PK reports – tables with Cmax, AUC, t½); TK sections embedded within Module 4.2.3.2 repeat-dose reports (search “toxicokinetics”).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: For each species, route, and study, compare Cmax and AUC values in Module 2.6.3 and tabulated Module 2.6.4 vs the original TK/PK tables in 4.2.2.x and TK sections in 4.2.3.2. Allow for rounding but flag differences >10–20% or inconsistent units.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Incorrect TK values compromise exposure-multiple calculations and starting dose justification.

Consistency Checks.Description: Exposure multiple vs clinical dose inconsistency
Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.3, 2.4.5 (statements like “~10-fold safety margin”); Module 2.6.3 and 2.6.4 (tables listing “multiple vs clinical exposure”, “fold human”); Module 4.2.2.x (animal TK/PK parameters used in those multiples).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: Verify that exposure multiples reported in 2.4.3/2.4.5 and 2.6.3/2.6.4 are mathematically consistent with AUC/Cmax values extracted from 4.2.2.x for the stated clinical reference exposure (e.g., intended clinical Cmax/AUC). Flag if calculated multiples do not match (e.g., textual “10-fold” but calculated ~3-fold).
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Miscalculated exposure multiples (e.g., AUC animal / AUC human) directly affect regulatory acceptance of the starting and escalation doses.

Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.4 (Toxicology overview – “NOAEL”); Module 2.4.5 (Integrated overview – NOAEL and margins); Module 2.6.5.2 (Repeat-dose written – “NOAEL”, “NOEL”); Module 2.6.6.2 (Repeat-dose tabulated – NOAEL column); Module 4.2.3.2 (repeat-dose study discussion, conclusions).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: For each pivotal repeat-dose study, compare the NOAEL dose stated in Module 2.4.4/2.4.5, 2.6.5.2 text, and the NOAEL column in 2.6.6.2 with the conclusion in the corresponding Module 4.2.3.2 report. Flag if any module lists a different NOAEL (e.g., 30 mg/kg vs 100 mg/kg) for the same study.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Conflicting NOAEL dose undermines the fundamental basis for first-in-human dose selection and risk assessment.

Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.3, 2.4.5 (statements like “NOAEL AUC was X μg·h/mL”); Module 2.6.3/2.6.4 (tables of TK/PK at NOAEL); Module 2.6.6.2 (columns for “AUC at NOAEL”, “Cmax at NOAEL”); Module 4.2.2.x TK reports; TK sections in 4.2.3.2.
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: For each pivotal study, compare AUC and Cmax at the NOAEL in Modules 2.6.3/2.6.4 and 2.6.6.2 vs original TK data in Module 4.2.2.x and TK sections of 4.2.3.2. Ensure the exposure values correspond to the same nominal dose and sampling schedule. Flag mismatches in magnitude or units (e.g., ng·h/mL vs μg·h/mL).
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: If exposure at the NOAEL is mis-stated, margins vs clinical exposure are incorrect even if the dose is right.

Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.4, 2.4.5 (mentions of “MTD”, “maximum tolerated dose”, “dose-limiting toxicity”); Module 2.6.5.1–2.6.5.2 (MTD description); Module 4.2.3.1–4.2.3.2 (summary/discussion of “DLT”, “MTD”).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: Compare how MTD is defined (e.g., mortality threshold, severe clinical signs, predefined criteria) in Module 2.4.4/2.4.5 and 2.6.5.x vs the explicit description in Module 4.2.3.1–4.2.3.2. Flag if summaries call a dose “MTD” when report text describes minimal or acceptable toxicity or if different doses are labeled MTD for the same study.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Different MTD definitions across sections suggest selective interpretation and can weaken confidence in dose selection.

Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.4 (target organ list); Module 2.4.5 (integrated target organ safety conclusions); Module 2.6.5.2 (repeat-dose toxicity findings); Module 2.6.6.2 (tables of “target organs”); Module 4.2.3.2 (findings in Results/Discussion across all tissues).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: For each organ with treatment-related findings in Module 4.2.3.2 (histopathology tables, clinical chemistry, etc.), check that the organ appears as a target organ in 2.6.5.2 and in the integrated list in 2.4.4/2.4.5. Flag if significant, consistent findings (e.g., liver hypertrophy/necrosis, cardiac changes) are omitted or downgraded.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Under-reporting target organs in integrated summaries can mislead clinical monitoring plans and risk assessment.

Consistency Checks.Description: Serious toxicities / mortality downplayed or omitted
Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.4, 2.4.5 (statements like “no mortality”, “well tolerated”); Module 2.6.5.1–2.6.5.2 (narratives of mortality and severe clinical signs); Module 2.6.6.1–2.6.6.2 (tables: “deaths”, “moribund”); Module 4.2.3.1–4.2.3.2 (Results – “mortality”, “unscheduled deaths”).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: Compare statements about mortality and severe toxicity (e.g., seizures, anaphylaxis, marked hypotension) in Module 2.4.4/2.4.5 and 2.6.5.x with detailed mortality tables and narratives in 4.2.3.1–4.2.3.2. Flag if summaries claim “no deaths” when deaths are reported, or if serious adverse effects are described as “mild” or “non-adverse” contrary to report descriptions.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Failure to transparently describe deaths and severe toxicities can trigger serious FDA concern or hold.

Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.4, 2.4.5 (text containing “reversible”, “recovered”, “persistent”); Module 2.6.5.2 (Repeat-dose written – “recovery phase”, “satellite group”); Module 2.6.6.2 (columns for “Reversibility”); Module 4.2.3.2 (Results – recovery group data).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: For each study with a recovery period, compare statements about reversibility in Modules 2.4.4/2.4.5 and 2.6.5.2/2.6.6.2 with actual findings in Module 4.2.3.2 (recovery group histopathology, clinical pathology). Flag when summary says “findings fully reversed” but residual lesions or changes are documented.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Overstating reversibility can inappropriately reassure about long-term risk and affect monitoring duration.

Consistency Checks.Description: Group size / sex / recovery group mismatch
Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.6.5.1–2.6.5.2 (design descriptions – “n per group”, “males/females”); Module 2.6.6.1–2.6.6.2 (columns for animals per group, recovery groups); Module 4.2.3.1–4.2.3.2 (Study design tables).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: For each study, compare numbers of animals per group, sex distribution, and presence/size of recovery groups in 2.6.5.x and 2.6.6.x vs 4.2.3.1–4.2.3.2 design tables. Flag if group sizes are over-stated in 2.6.x or if recovery groups claimed in summaries are not present in the reports.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Misreported group sizes or absence/presence of recovery groups affects the perceived robustness of the data set.

Consistency Checks.Description: Protocol deviations and early terminations unreported in summaries
Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.4, 2.4.5 (any mention of deviations/limitations); Module 2.6.5.1–2.6.5.2 (text around “deviations”, “early termination”, “stopped early”); Module 4.2.3.1–4.2.3.2 (sections “Protocol deviations”, “Amendments”, “Termination of study”).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: Search Module 4.2.3.1–4.2.3.2 for major deviations or early terminations; check whether these are acknowledged in 2.6.5.x and, if impactful, in 2.4.4/2.4.5. Flag if major issues (e.g., early termination of high-dose group) are not mentioned anywhere in summaries.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Omission of major deviations or early termination can overstate study reliability and completeness.

Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.2 (pharmacology – species target binding/PD), 2.4.3 (PK differences), 2.4.4–2.4.5 (toxicology and overall species relevance statements); Module 2.6.1, 2.6.3, 2.6.5.x (species-specific data); Module 4.2.1–4.2.3 (all pharmacology/PK/tox reports).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: Identify statements in 2.4.4/2.4.5 about “most relevant species” or “most sensitive species” and compare to species patterns in 2.6.1/2.6.3/2.6.5.x and 4.2.1–4.2.3 (e.g., which species shows highest exposure or toxicity). Flag if a species is labeled “most relevant” but has minimal PD or markedly different target biology vs another well-studied species.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Misalignment between narrative about “most relevant” or “most sensitive” species and actual findings may distort clinical species selection and margin.

Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.2 (pharmacology overview – “disease model”, “target engagement”); Module 2.6.1 (primary pharmacodynamics) and 2.6.2 (secondary pharmacodynamics, safety pharmacology); Module 4.2.1 (pharmacology study reports).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: Compare claims in Module 2.4.2 (e.g., “model predicts clinical efficacy”, “relevant to human disease”) with the actual model description and results in 2.6.1/2.6.2 and 4.2.1. Flag if the model species, route, or endpoints in 4.2.1 do not match what is described as “key” or “predictive” in 2.4.2.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Overstating translational relevance of pharmacology models can bias perceived benefit–risk.

Consistency Checks.Description: Missing or inconsistent safety pharmacology coverage
Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.2 (mentions of CV, CNS, respiratory effects); Module 2.6.1/2.6.2 (safety pharmacology written/tabulated – search “hERG”, “QTc”, “respiration”, “locomotor”); Module 4.2.1.x (safety pharmacology study reports); ECG, respiratory, CNS endpoints within 4.2.3.2 repeat-dose studies (where safety pharm is embedded).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: Confirm that each safety pharmacology area claimed as “completed” in 2.6.1/2.6.2 has corresponding reports or embedded endpoints in 4.2.1.x or 4.2.3.2. Compare key findings (e.g., QTc prolongation, blood pressure effects, seizures) in 4.2.1/4.2.3.2 with narrative in 2.4.2/2.4.4. Flag if significant safety pharm findings are omitted or if claims of “no effect on QTc” contradict 4.2.1/4.2.3.2 data.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Lack or misrepresentation of core safety pharmacology (CV, CNS, respiratory) is a common basis for IRs or holds.

Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.2 (secondary pharmacology/off-target discussion); Module 2.6.1/2.6.2 (secondary pharmacodynamics, broad receptor/enzyme panels); Module 4.2.1.x (secondary pharmacology / broad screening reports).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: Search 4.2.1.x for off-target hits (e.g., hERG, CNS receptors) and compare to how they are described in 2.4.2 and 2.6.1/2.6.2. Flag if strong or moderate off-target effects linked to safety concerns are omitted or mischaracterized as “no meaningful activity”.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Failure to mention concerning off-target activities (e.g., ion channels, enzyme inhibition) may hide mechanistic safety concerns.

Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.4, 2.4.5 (local tolerance statements); Module 2.6.5.6 (Local tolerance written summary); Module 2.6.6.6 (Local tolerance tabulated – “erythema”, “edema”, “necrosis”); Module 4.2.3.6 (Local tolerance reports) and local-site sections of 4.2.3.2.
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: Compare local tolerance findings (e.g., scoring of erythema, edema, ulceration, histopathology at injection site) in 4.2.3.6 and relevant 4.2.3.2 sections with the summary in 2.6.5.6 and 2.4.4/2.4.5. Flag if frequent or severe local findings (e.g., ulceration, necrosis) are minimized or not mentioned.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Under-reporting injection-site or local reactions can affect route feasibility and patient monitoring plans.

Consistency Checks.Description: Immunogenicity / immune findings inconsistency (biologics or immunogenic small molecules)
Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.4, 2.4.5 (mentions “ADA”, “immunogenicity”, “cytokine release”, “immune complex”); Module 2.6.3 (PK impacts of ADA), 2.6.5.2/2.6.5.7 (immune findings in toxicity or “other toxicity studies”); Module 2.6.6.2/2.6.6.7 (tables listing ADA incidence, immune findings); Module 4.2.2.x (ADA/TK reports); Module 4.2.3.2/4.2.3.7 (immune endpoints, cytokine panels, pathology).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: Compare ADA incidence and impact on TK reported in 4.2.2.x and 4.2.3.2/4.2.3.7 with the narrative in 2.4.4/2.4.5 and 2.6.3/2.6.5.x. Flag if significant ADA effects (loss of exposure, hypersensitivity, immune complex disease) seen in 4.2.x are minimized or absent in the summaries.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Mischaracterizing ADA or immune activation can lead to unexpected loss of exposure or immune-mediated toxicity in humans.

Consistency Checks.Description: Special risk findings (e.g., hypersensitivity, cytokine release) omitted
Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.4, 2.4.5 (text containing “hypersensitivity”, “anaphylaxis”, “cytokine”, “infusion reaction”); Module 2.6.5.2/2.6.5.7 (immune findings in repeat-dose/other tox); Module 4.2.3.2/4.2.3.7 (clinical signs, cytokine panels, necropsy findings suggesting immune reactions).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: Search 4.2.3.2/4.2.3.7 for terms indicating hypersensitivity or cytokine release (e.g., “anaphylactoid”, “cytokine storm”, “mast cell degranulation”), and verify these phenomena are clearly described in 2.6.5.x and 2.4.4/2.4.5. Flag omissions or strong downplaying.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Omission of serious immune/hypersensitivity phenomena can be directly relevant to early clinical safety.

Consistency Checks.Description: Conflicting findings across studies not acknowledged
Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.4, 2.4.5 (integrated tox discussion); Module 2.6.5.2 (per-study repeat-dose findings); Module 2.6.6.2 (per-study tables); Module 4.2.3.2 (all repeat-dose reports across species/durations).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: Identify organs/findings that are present in some repeat-dose studies in 4.2.3.2 but absent in others (e.g., liver toxicity in dogs but not rats). Check if 2.4.4/2.4.5 and 2.6.5.2 explicitly discuss these discrepancies (species, dose, duration, exposure differences). Flag when conflicts exist but integrated sections present a simplified “no consistent toxicity” narrative.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: When one study shows toxicity and another does not, integrated summaries must explain why; ignoring conflict undermines credibility.

Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.4, 2.4.5 (mentions “sex differences”, “species differences”); Module 2.6.5.2 and 2.6.6.2 (tables by sex and species); Module 4.2.3.2 (Results by sex and species).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: Compare sex- and species-stratified findings in 4.2.3.2 with the integrated discussion in 2.4.4/2.4.5. Flag if repeated, clear sex or species differences (e.g., males only renal toxicity) are not mentioned or are inaccurately stated (e.g., summary claims “no sex differences”).
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Sex- or species-specific signals may be critical for labeling and clinical monitoring; ignoring them can be problematic.

Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.4 (per-study and per-species NOAEL); Module 2.4.5 (overall NOAEL used for margin calculations); Module 2.6.5.2 (per-study NOAEL in text); Module 2.6.6.2 (NOAEL column).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: Within Modules 2.4.x and 2.6.x, compare all NOAEL/NOEL mentions for each study and species. Flag internal inconsistencies (e.g., 2.4.4 states 30 mg/kg as NOAEL, 2.4.5 or 2.6.5.2 uses 10 mg/kg for the same study, or multiple NOAELs given without explanation).
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Different NOAEL values in different parts of Module 2 create confusion and delay review.

Consistency Checks.Description: Internal exposure margin inconsistencies within Module 2
Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.3, 2.4.5 (tables/text with “fold safety margin”, “X-fold above clinical exposure”); Module 2.6.3/2.6.4 (PK multiples vs human exposure); Module 2.6.6.2 (exposure at NOAEL and corresponding multiples).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: For each key species and study, compare reported fold-margins in 2.4.3/2.4.5 with those implied by TK values and multiples in 2.6.3/2.6.4/2.6.6.2. Flag if different multiples (e.g., 30-fold vs 50-fold) are given for the same NOAEL and clinical reference without explanation.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Differing exposure multiples can suggest calculation or unit errors and trigger detailed IRs.

Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.4 (genotoxicity overview); Module 2.6.5.3 (Genotoxicity written summary); Module 2.6.6.3 (Genotoxicity tabulated – “Result”, “Positive/Negative”, “Equivocal”); Module 4.2.3.3 (Genotoxicity study reports – Ames, micronucleus, chromosomal aberration).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: For each genotoxicity assay, compare results in Module 2.6.5.3/2.6.6.3 and summary in 2.4.4 vs the conclusion in the original report (4.2.3.3). Flag if a positive or equivocal result in 4.2.3.3 is reported as negative in the summaries, or if key assay conditions (e.g., metabolic activation) are misrepresented.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Misreporting genotox outcomes (positive vs negative) directly affects carcinogenic risk assessment and may alter development plans.

Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.4, 2.4.5 (reproductive risk statements); Module 2.6.5.5 (Reproductive and developmental toxicity written); Module 2.6.6.5 (tabulated outcomes); Module 4.2.3.5 (fertility, embryo–fetal, pre/postnatal reports).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: For each repro/developmental study, compare malformation, embryo-fetal death, and fertility findings in 4.2.3.5 with summary statements and tabulated outcomes in 2.6.5.5/2.6.6.5 and the overall risk description in 2.4.4/2.4.5. Flag if significant findings are downgraded or omitted.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Misrepresenting reproductive/developmental risk affects contraception recommendations and inclusion of women of childbearing potential.

Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.4, 2.4.5 (carcinogenicity/tumorigenicity statements); Module 2.6.5.4 (Carcinogenicity written); Module 2.6.6.4 (Carcinogenicity tabulated); Module 4.2.3.4 (carcinogenicity studies) and 4.2.3.7 (tumorigenicity/long-term studies, esp. for cell/gene therapies).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: Compare any tumor/tumorigenicity findings reported in 4.2.3.4/4.2.3.7 with how these are summarized in 2.6.5.4/2.6.6.4 and 2.4.4/2.4.5. Flag omission or re-labeling of clear test-article-related tumors as “spontaneous” without support.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: For longer programs or certain modalities, omission of tumorigenicity data can be a serious concern.

Consistency Checks.Description: Biologics: ADA impact on exposure and toxicity misaligned
Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.3, 2.4.4 (PK and tox overview – “ADA”, “anti-drug antibodies”); Module 2.6.3 (PK and ADA), 2.6.5.2/2.6.5.7 (ADA-related tox findings); Module 2.6.6.2/2.6.6.7 (ADA incidence tables); Module 4.2.2.x (ADA and PK reports); Module 4.2.3.2/4.2.3.7 (ADA-related clinical signs/pathology).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: Compare ADA incidence and magnitude (e.g., titre ranges) in 4.2.2.x and 4.2.3.2/4.2.3.7 to tables and text in 2.6.3/2.6.6.x. Verify that statements in 2.4.3/2.4.4 about ADA impact on exposure and toxicity (e.g., “no meaningful impact”) are consistent with observed changes in TK and tox. Flag contradictions.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: For biologics, ADA can dramatically alter exposure and toxicity; inconsistent handling can lead to wrong margin assumptions.

Consistency Checks.Description: Biologics: Cytokine release / CRS risk misrepresented
Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.4.2, 2.4.4, 2.4.5 (statements about cytokine release, CRS risk); Module 2.6.1/2.6.2 (in vitro and in vivo cytokine assays); Module 2.6.5.2/2.6.5.7 (cytokine findings in tox studies); Module 4.2.1 (ex vivo cytokine assays), 4.2.3.2/4.2.3.7 (cytokine panels in vivo).
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: Compare cytokine elevation data in in vitro and in vivo studies (4.2.1, 4.2.3.2, 4.2.3.7) with how CRS risk is described in 2.4.4/2.4.5 and 2.6.1/2.6.5.x. Flag if substantial cytokine spikes or CRS-like clinical signs in 4.2.x are minimized or missing in Module 2 summaries.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: For immune-modulating biologics, mischaracterizing cytokine release risk is directly relevant to clinical safety (e.g., premedication, dose ramp-up).

Consistency Checks.Description: Minor numeric / rounding inconsistencies in tables
Consistency Checks.Where to check: Module 2.6.3/2.6.4 (PK tables); Module 2.6.6.x (tox tables – NOAEL, exposure); Module 4.2.2.x and 4.2.3.x tables.
Consistency Checks.Specific checks: Check that numeric values in Module 2 tables are within an acceptable rounding range (e.g., ±5–10%) of the corresponding values in Module 4 tables. Flag only when differences are obviously rounding or transcription errors with no impact on interpretation.
Consistency Checks.Why it matters: Small numeric differences can cause confusion but rarely alter regulatory decisions if margins remain adequate.
